accepted.question_text: Determine the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane: what is the smallest integer c such that every point of the plane can be assigned one of c colors with the property that any two points at Euclidean distance exactly 1 receive different colors? Equivalently, determine the maximum chromatic number possible for a unit-distance graph, meaning a graph whose vertices can be embedded as points in the plane with every edge represented by a unit-length segment. The source states that the answer is known to lie among 4, 5, 6, and 7, so the open task is to decide which value is correct; a closely related intermediate goal mentioned in the collection is to construct a 7-coloring of the plane, which would improve the stated 9-color upper-bound illustration to the best-known upper bound of 7.

evidence.quote: How many colors are needed so that if each point in the plane is assigned one of the colors, no two points which are exactly distance 1 apart will be assigned the same color? This problem has been open since 1956. It is known that the answer is either 4, 5, 6 or 7---this is not too hard to show. ... A graph which can be embedded in the plane so that vertices correspond to points in the plane and edges correspond to unit-length line segments is called a ``unit-distance graph.'' The question above is equivalent to asking what the chromatic number of unit-distance graphs can be.

Assign a color to each point of the plane so that pairs of points whose distance is exactly 1 get different colors. The minimum number of colors required to achieve this is called the "chromatic number of the plane," and noone knows what it is. ... At that time, it was proved that the chromatic number of the plane was either 4, 5, 6 or 7, and no improvements on those bounds have been made since! ... Can you find a coloring with 7 colors to get the current best-known upper bound?

accepted.question_text: For unit-distance graphs that require 4 colors, determine how small such graphs can be when one also imposes large girth, and determine whether there exist 4-chromatic unit-distance graphs of arbitrarily large girth. The source records examples of girths 4 and 5 on 23 and 45 vertices respectively, and a non-3-colorable unit-distance graph of girth 12 with an extremely large number of vertices, so the open problem is to improve these constructions or prove existence for unbounded girth.

evidence.quote: In this problem, we are interested in finding what sort of unit-distance graphs we can make--in particular, can we find 4-chromatic graphs which have large girth? ... Hochberg and O'Donnell have found 4-chromatic unit-distance graphs of girths 4 and 5 with 23 ... and 45 vertices respectively. Are there smaller ones? Are there 4-chromatic unit-distance graphs of arbitrarily large girth?

accepted.question_text: Is every 3-connected, 3-regular, planar bipartite graph Hamiltonian? The source notes that the analogous statement becomes false if the bipartite hypothesis is removed, so the open issue is whether the bipartite restriction is strong enough to force a Hamiltonian cycle in every graph in this class.

evidence.quote: Is it true that every 3-connected, 3-regular, planar bipartite graph is Hamiltonian? It is known that this is not true if you remove the "bipartite" condition, but the smallest known such graph which is not Hamiltonian has 38 vertices

accepted.question_text: Determine the crossing number of the complete bipartite graph K(9,9): among all plane drawings of K(9,9) in which edges are drawn as curves that meet vertices only at endpoints and no three curves pass through the same point, what is the minimum possible number of edge crossings? The source says 256 is conjectured, but unknown.

evidence.quote: What is the crossing number of the complete bipartite graph K(9, 9)? It is conjectured to be 256, but nobody knows. ... If you place 9 red points in the plane and 9 blue points in the plane, and then connect each red point to each blue point with curves (81 curves in all), then what is the minimum number of crossing points that must appear in your drawing? ... For these drawings, it is assumed that the curves do not touch the points (vertices) except at their endpoints, and that no three curves meet at a point.

accepted.question_text: For an integer k greater than 1, does every k-connected graph that has no Hamiltonian cycle necessarily contain a cycle that includes k pairwise independent vertices together with all of their neighbors? The source says this statement is known for k = 2 and k = 3, and asks whether it continues to hold for all larger k.
accepted.context_brief: Cycles capturing independent vertices and neighbors

evidence.quote: Is it true that every k-connected (k>1) graph which does not have a Hamiltonian cycle has a cycle that contains k independent vertices and their neighbors? This is known to be true for k = 2 and 3.

accepted.question_text: Let D be an oriented graph, meaning a simple directed graph obtained from a simple undirected graph by orienting each edge so that no pair of opposite directed edges occurs. Form the square of D by keeping the same vertex set, keeping all existing arcs, and adding an arc (u,w) whenever D contains arcs (u,v) and (v,w) and the arc (u,w) is not already present. Must there always exist a vertex whose out-degree at least doubles when passing from D to its square?

evidence.quote: Here is the open problem: Prove that for every oriented graph, D, there exists a vertex whose out-degree at least doubles when you square the oriented graph. ... David Fisher proved this theorem for tournaments, i.e., orientations of complete graphs.

accepted.question_text: Given N points in the plane in general position, meaning no three are collinear, draw the segment joining every pair of points. What lower bound must always hold on the size of a family of pairwise mutually crossing segments? More specifically, the source states that one can always guarantee a crossing family of size sqrt(N/12), and asks for the largest exponent t such that every such N-point set contains a crossing family of at least cN^t segments for some fixed positive constant c. In particular, any proof with t greater than 1/2 would improve the known exponent.

evidence.quote: Consider N points in the plane so that no three points lie on a line. Draw a line segment between each pair of vertices. The open problem is this: How large a family of mutually crossing line segments must there be? ... It has been shown that there must always be a family of size sqrt(N/12), but it is believed that there must always be families of much larger size as well. So, what is the largest exponent t so that among N points in the plane, no three on a line, one can always find a crossing family of at least cN^t line segments, for some fixed constant c>0?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an integer N with the property that every set of at least N points in the plane in general position, meaning no three points lie on one line, must contain an empty hexagon: six points that are the vertices of a convex hexagon whose interior contains no point of the set?

evidence.quote: The following question of Erdos remains open: "Is there an integer N such that any set of at least N points in the plane, no three on a line, contains an empty hexagon (i.e., six vertices of a convex hexagon whose interior contains no point of the set)?"

accepted.question_text: Fix a sufficiently large integer K. Must every set of K^2 points contained in a K by K square, with pairwise distances at least 1/10, contain an empty hexagon? Here an empty hexagon means six of the points form a convex hexagon whose interior contains no point of the set. The source presents this as a potentially easier restricted variant of the general empty-hexagon problem.

evidence.quote: Could you at least find, for any sufficiently large integer K, an empty hexagon in any set of K^2 points in a square K by K, when the distance between any two points is at least 1/10, say. This could be easier, although there is an example of such restricted sets with no empty heptagon.

accepted.question_text: Let S be a set of N^2 points inside a disk whose boundary circle C has length N, and assume any two points of S are at distance at least 1/100. Let A be a set of N^2 points spaced equally along C. The source states that for at least c·N^4 ordered pairs a,b from A, some point of S lies within distance 1/N of the line through a and b, for a fixed positive constant c. Must there exist a positive constant d such that for at least d·N^4 pairs a,b from A, there are at least two points of S within distance 1/N of the line ab?

evidence.quote: Consider a set S of N^2 points inside a disk bounded by a circle C of length N, such that the distance between any two points of S is at least 1/100, say. Let A be a set of N^2 points distributed equidistantly along C. It is known that for at least c·N^4 pairs a,b of points of A, there is a point of S at distance at most 1/N from the line ab (c>0 is a positive constant). Is there a positive constant d>0 such that for at least d·N^4 pairs a,b of points of A, there are at least two points of S at distance at most 1/N from the line ab?

accepted.question_text: How large can a finite set of points on the half-parabola y = x^2 with x > 0 be if every pairwise Euclidean distance among the chosen points is rational? The source says it is not even known whether more than five such points exist. It further asks whether there is an infinite family of points on this half-parabola with all pairwise distances rational, and notes that any configuration with rational pairwise distances can be converted into one with integer pairwise distances.

evidence.quote: The problems is this: How many points can you find on the (half) parabola y=x^2, x>0, so that the distance between any pair of them is rational? ... I believe it is not even known if there are more than 5 points on the parabola which satisfy the condition. It is certainly not known if there is an infinite family with pairwise rational distances. ... It is not too hard to show that if you have N points on the parabola with rational distances between them, then you can find N points on the parabola with integer distances between them.

accepted.question_text: Is it possible to construct a Venn diagram using 6 triangles? In the source's terminology, a Venn diagram on n closed curves is one in which each of the 2^n subsets of the curves corresponds to a unique region lying inside exactly that subset. The page notes that diagrams with 5 triangles are possible, while the existence of one with 6 triangles is open.

evidence.quote: It is possible to create a Venn diagram with 5 triangles, but this is tricky. The open problem is this: is it possible to create a Venn diagram with 6 triangles?

accepted.question_text: Is every simple Venn diagram extendable to a larger simple Venn diagram by adding one more curve? Here 'simple' means that whenever curves meet they cross rather than being tangent, and no three curves meet at a single point. The source says this is Peter Winkler's conjecture and explains that, if one views the Venn diagram as a planar graph whose vertices are curve intersections and whose edges are curve-arcs between consecutive intersections, the conjecture is equivalent to asserting that the dual graph of any simple Venn diagram is Hamiltonian.

evidence.quote: A Venn diagram is called "simple" if curves cross when they meet (no tangencies) and if no 3 curves meet at a point. ... Winkler conjectured about 15 years ago that any simple Venn diagram could be extended to a larger simple Venn diagram with the addition of a single curve. ... Winkler's conjecture amounts to showing that the dual of this graph is Hamiltonian. ... So, to prove Winkler's conjecture, you can prove that the dual graph to any simple Venn diagram is Hamiltonian.
